prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "Broadcom Inc." (ticker AVGO). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: Broadcom has several Rule Breaker traits: it leads a major trend as the top designer of custom AI chips and AI Ethernet, it has strong partners in Google, Anthropic and OpenAI, and critics often call it expensive. Its recent price action is weak, though. The stock is up 10.1% over 52 weeks against the S&P 500's 20.4% total return and is about 28% below its 52-week high of $495.00. Its growth comes largely from acquisitions, which makes it more of a Rule Maker than a classic Rule Breaker.
summaries.buffett: Buffett would admire Broadcom's franchise chip and software businesses, its 75.5% gross margin and its strong free cash flow of $39.4B over the last twelve months (StockAnalysis). He would be cautious about the fast-changing technology, its dependence on a few AI customers, its use of debt for acquisitions ($59.4B of debt) and a trailing P/E of 45.6. It is a high-quality business but sits outside his usual comfort zone on predictability and price.
summaries.munger: Munger would recognise Hock Tan's rational, unsentimental capital allocation and the strong niche positions in switching, custom chips and VMware. Inverting the question shows clear risks: customer concentration, the AI capex cycle, Nvidia's competition and VMware customer backlash. It is a great business with notable fragility in its AI growth.
summaries.lynch: To Lynch Broadcom would be a fast grower riding AI, with a PEG of only 0.38 on forward estimates (StockAnalysis), which he would find attractive. Its story is simple for a chip company: custom AI chips plus networking plus sticky software. It is widely followed, and insiders sell rather than buy.
summaries.fisher: Broadcom fits Fisher well on R&D results, strong margins and selling to the world's biggest technology buyers, with AI semiconductor revenue up 221% to $16.7B in Q3 FY2026. Fisher would ask about labour relations after deep layoffs at acquired companies, and about whether its growth by acquisition reflects innovation of its own. It qualifies as a strong long-term growth stock.
summaries.graham: Broadcom fails Graham's defensive tests: it had a net loss in fiscal 2016, it has paid dividends only since 2010, and its P/E of 45.6 times its P/B of 17.1 is about 780. Its size is the only criterion it clearly meets.
summaries.thiel: Broadcom answers several of Thiel's questions well: it has proprietary engineering in SerDes, packaging and switch chips, its timing in AI is excellent, and it holds near-monopoly niches. Thiel would see its acquisition-based model as distribution and capital skill more than a single 'zero to one' secret. Its long-term position depends on whether hyperscalers keep outsourcing chip design.
summaries.gerstner: Broadcom fits Gerstner's focus on the leading beneficiaries of AI compute, and its lean cost structure (about 66% non-GAAP operating margin) matches his call for efficiency. A forward P/E of about 20.6 is reasonable if AI revenue guidance (about $115B for FY2027) is met. The risk is the AI capex cycle.
summaries.druckenmiller: Earnings are accelerating sharply (trailing EPS of $7.83 against $4.77 for FY2025), which Druckenmiller likes, but the price trend has broken. The stock fell about 15% in a day in June 2026 on AI guidance and Google TPU share concerns and fell again after the September guidance, ending about 28% below its high. He would likely wait for the trend to recover before sizing up.
summaries.smith: Broadcom meets several of Terry Smith's tests: a high gross margin (75.5%), ROIC of about 31% (StockAnalysis) and strong cash conversion. Smith would dislike its reliance on large debt-funded acquisitions and its cyclical semiconductor exposure, which conflict with his preference for predictable, low-debt compounders.
summaries.greenblatt: Broadcom scores well on return on capital but poorly on earnings yield, with EV/EBIT of about 40 (StockAnalysis) on GAAP figures held down by acquisition amortisation. It would not rank highly on the Magic Formula today.
summaries.akre: Broadcom fits Akre's three-legged stool in part: an excellent, high-return business and a proven capital allocator in Hock Tan, whose pay is tied to AI revenue targets. The reinvestment leg relies on acquisitions and AI demand rather than steady organic compounding, and that is less of a fit for Akre.
summaries.pabrai: Broadcom is not a classic Dhandho bet: it is not a simple, distressed business, and the market already prices in high AI growth. The stock's fall of about 28% from its high creates some opportunity, but the downside is not clearly limited if AI spending slows.
summaries.wood: Broadcom is a key AI hardware enabler, which fits ARK's AI theme, and custom accelerators lower AI compute costs for hyperscalers. It is a picks-and-shovels supplier with one main innovation platform rather than a company combining several, so it fits ARK's convergence idea only in part.
summaries.ackman: Broadcom partly fits Ackman's criteria: dominant niches, high barriers to entry, strong free cash flow and a shareholder-focused CEO. It is less simple and predictable than he prefers because AI chip demand is cyclical and concentrated among a few customers, and its debt is substantial.
summaries.sleep: Broadcom is a weak fit for Nick Sleep's 'scale economies shared' idea. It uses its scale to raise prices, most clearly at VMware, rather than passing savings to customers. Its custom chips do let hyperscalers avoid paying Nvidia's margins, which shares some savings with them.
summaries.valentine: Valentine would like the size of the AI data-centre market and the hard technical problems Broadcom solves. As a $1.7T company built by acquisitions it is far from Sequoia's early-stage focus, but the problem it addresses (moving and processing AI data at scale) is large and painful.

momentum.evidence: AVGO closed at $357.31 on 13 October 2026, up 10.1% over 52 weeks versus SPY's 20.4% total return, and about 28% below its 52-week high of $495.00.

g4.evidence: CEO Hock Tan has led it since 2006, and its partners include Google (TPUs), Anthropic and OpenAI under multi-gigawatt agreements.

g6.evidence: Critics often point to its 45.6 trailing P/E and 17.1 price-to-book (StockAnalysis), and the stock fell about 15% in one day in June 2026 partly on valuation concerns.

simple.evidence: The two segments (semiconductors and infrastructure software) are clear, but custom AI chip deals and acquisition accounting are hard for a generalist to evaluate.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $23.9B in FY2020 to $63.9B in FY2025, though GAAP net income has been uneven (for example $5.9B in FY2024).

integrity.evidence: Hock Tan is a rational capital allocator whose pay is tied to AI revenue targets through 2030, but steep VMware price rises have drawn customer lawsuits and regulatory scrutiny.

b6.evidence: Broadcom avoids fads and runs a disciplined strategy, but it grew through very large acquisitions (CA, Symantec, VMware) that could be seen as empire-building.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 31% and ROE about 44% (StockAnalysis), but returns rely partly on $59.4B of debt taken on for acquisitions.

fcf.evidence: Trailing free cash flow was $39.4B against net income of $38.3B (StockAnalysis), so it turns essentially all its profit into cash.

b10.evidence: Revenue grew from about $1.5B at Avago's 2009 IPO to $63.9B in FY2025 and market value to about $1.7T, well above the capital retained and borrowed.

safety.evidence: At 45.6 times trailing earnings and 17.1 times book (StockAnalysis) there is no conservative margin of safety, even after the stock fell from its high.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of 20.6 and PEG of 0.38 (StockAnalysis) look reasonable for growth of over 60% in FY2026, if AI forecasts hold.

mu5.evidence: Its main ways to fail are clear: concentration on a few AI customers, the AI capex cycle, supply limits at TSMC and VMware customer defections.

reinvest.evidence: AI chips offer large high-return reinvestment for now, but Broadcom historically deploys cash through acquisitions and dividends rather than steady organic reinvestment.

ly2.evidence: It is a fast grower with a simple story: hyperscalers buy custom AI chips and Ethernet switches from Broadcom, while VMware supplies steady software cash.

ly3.evidence: The PEG ratio is 0.38 on forward estimates (StockAnalysis), so the P/E is well below the expected earnings growth rate.

runway.evidence: Management guides AI semiconductor revenue to about $115B in FY2027 and about $230B in FY2028, compared with about $106B of total revenue expected in FY2026.

ly7.evidence: The share count rose 0.99% year on year (StockAnalysis), and insiders own only about 1% and have been sellers.

ly8.evidence: Broadcom is a core AI holding covered by about 50 analysts (StockAnalysis).

fi2.evidence: It keeps launching new generations (Tomahawk 6 and Tomahawk Ultra, 3.5D XDSiP packaging, co-packaged optics) and moved into rack-scale AI systems.

fi3.evidence: Its R&D produced the first 102.4 Tbps switch chip and the custom XPUs behind Google's TPUs, and AI revenue grew 221% in Q3 FY2026.

fi4.evidence: It wins multi-gigawatt deals with the largest AI buyers, but it sells to a small number of customers and many VMware clients resent its sales tactics.

longterm.evidence: Broadcom invests in multi-generation chip roadmaps, but Hock Tan's model emphasises near-term margins and cost cuts after acquisitions.

gr1.evidence: Revenue was $63.9B in FY2025, about $106B is expected for FY2026, and market value is about $1.7T.

ni10.evidence: Broadcom reported a net loss attributable to ordinary shares of $1,739M in fiscal 2016.

gr4.evidence: Avago began paying dividends around 2010, fewer than 20 years ago, though it has raised the dividend for 15 straight years.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $4.85 in FY2015 (about $0.49 after the 2024 10-for-1 split) to $4.77 in FY2025.

gr6.evidence: Average EPS for FY2023-FY2025 was about $3.10 ($3.30, $1.23, $4.77), so $357.31 is about 115 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: P/E of 45.6 times P/B of 17.1 (StockAnalysis) is about 780, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its SerDes, switch chips and packaging lead the industry, but Marvell, MediaTek and Nvidia compete, so the edge is not 10 times.

timing.evidence: The AI data-centre build-out is at full speed, and Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue reached $16.7B in Q3 FY2026, up 221% year on year.

th3.evidence: Avago built dominant shares in niches (RF filters, switch chips) and expanded through acquisitions, but it did not grow from one small market in Thiel's sense.

team.evidence: Hock Tan is widely seen as one of the best capital allocators in technology, having grown Avago/Broadcom from about $1.5B revenue at its 2009 IPO to $63.9B in FY2025.

th5.evidence: Deep co-design relationships with Google, Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI, and VMware's enterprise sales channel, give it strong distribution.

durable.evidence: Its networking and software positions look durable, but hyperscalers could bring chip design in-house or move to rivals, and Google's TPU share is reported to be shifting.

th7.evidence: It saw early that hyperscalers wanted custom silicon and open Ethernet for AI, but competitors now pursue the same opportunity.

trend.evidence: Broadcom is the leading designer of custom AI accelerators and AI Ethernet switches, one of the clearest beneficiaries of AI spending.

dr1.evidence: Trailing EPS is $7.83 against $4.77 in FY2025 (StockAnalysis), and management guides AI revenue to about $115B in FY2027.

dr2.evidence: New multi-gigawatt programmes with Anthropic and OpenAI in 2027 could lift results, but gross margin may fall as lower-margin XPUs and systems grow.

dr4.evidence: Abundant capital for AI data centres helps, but its $59.4B of debt and reliance on AI labs' financing make it sensitive to credit conditions.

dr6.evidence: FY2026 Q4 results in December 2026, FY2027 AI guidance and the start of Anthropic and OpenAI deployments are clear catalysts.

dr7.evidence: AI exposure is strong, but customer concentration and the broken price trend argue for caution about a concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin is about 75.5% (StockAnalysis), with VMware software above 90%.

fcfyield.evidence: The free-cash-flow yield is about 2.3% (StockAnalysis), modest but reasonable given expected growth of over 60% in FY2026.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 40 (EV about $1.74T, StockAnalysis), an earnings yield of about 2.5%.

pa2.evidence: The share price setback (about 28% below its high) reflects guidance and Google TPU share worries rather than a broken business, as AI revenue keeps growing.

pa4.evidence: Strong cash flow and sticky VMware revenue limit risk, but a sharp AI capex slowdown could permanently reset expectations.

wo1.evidence: Broadcom is a leader in AI hardware through custom accelerators and AI networking.

wo2.evidence: Each switch and SerDes generation lowers cost per bit, and custom XPUs lower AI compute costs for buyers, which supports demand.

wo3.evidence: It focuses on AI and data-centre infrastructure and does not combine several ARK platforms such as robotics, energy storage or sequencing.

wo4.evidence: AI semiconductor revenue guidance of about $230B in FY2028 implies a much larger market, though not necessarily many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: It is insulated from commodities, but supply costs (TSMC wafers, substrates, HBM) and interest costs on $59.4B of debt affect it.

ns1.evidence: Broadcom uses its position to raise prices, most visibly the VMware licence increases after 2023, rather than passing scale savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: AI networking and custom silicon could make it stronger, but customer concentration and in-house chip efforts make that uncertain.

va2.evidence: It solves the large, painful problem of moving and processing enormous AI data volumes more cheaply than general-purpose GPUs.
